headline: Brazil votes for president and Congress on Sunday

sources.title: Brazil's 2026 Elections: Timeline and Fast Facts (AS/COA)
Lula and Bolsonaro's mudslinging heats up ahead of weekend vote (France 24)
Brazil vote approaches with Lula and Bolsonaro polling in close race (Reuters, via Investing.com)

chunks.text: Brazil holds a [[general election]] on Sunday, October 4, 2026. About 159 million people are [[eligible]] to vote. They will choose a president, state governors, all 513 members of the lower house of Congress and 54 of the 81 senators. Voting is [[compulsory]] for people aged 18 to 70. Those who do not {{show up}} have to pay a [[fine]]. Two of the 13 candidates for president have {{pulled ahead}} in the polls.

verbs.correct: To be present where you are expected
verbs.wrong: To leave the whole ballot empty
verbs.why: Only half the class showed up for the test. Our plumber never showed up on Saturday. In Brazil, voters aged 18 to 70 who do not show up on election day have to pay a fine.
Our team pulled ahead in the second half. One runner pulled ahead after the first mile. Of the 13 candidates for president, two have pulled ahead in the polls.

chunks.text: President Lula, who is 80, is seeking a fourth [[term]]. He {{faces off}} against Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator and the son of a former president. Under his current government, inflation and [[unemployment]] have {{come down}}. He has promised a more generous [[welfare program]] and [[debt relief]] for families. He has also promised to {{crack down on}} [[online betting]].

verbs.wrong: To accept a hard truth about yourself
verbs.why: The two best teams face off in the final tonight. Two chess champions faced off in a long match. President Lula faces off against Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator.
Gas prices have come down this month. Her fever came down overnight. Inflation and unemployment have come down under Lula's current government.

verbs.correct: To act strongly to stop something
verbs.wrong: To collect taxes from a business
verbs.why: The city is cracking down on illegal parking. The school cracked down on cheating during exams. Lula has promised to crack down on online betting.

chunks.text: Bolsonaro has made crime the center of his campaign. He has {{set out}} a plan to build five [[maximum-security prisons]] like those in El Salvador. Trade is another issue, because of US [[tariffs]] on Brazilian goods. His team says his ties with the Trump administration would protect Brazil. Lula says Brazil must {{stand up for}} its independence, including on trade with China. Both men are trying to {{win over}} voters who worry about crime, [[household debt]] and the [[cost of living]].

verbs.why: The coach set out her plan for the season. In the meeting, the manager set out three new goals. Bolsonaro has set out a plan to build five maximum-security prisons.

verbs.wrong: To be a short name for something
verbs.why: She always stands up for her friends. Workers stood up for their right to a lunch break. Lula says Brazil must stand up for its independence, including on trade with China.
The new teacher quickly won over the class. The restaurant won over its neighbors with free coffee. Both candidates are trying to win over voters who worry about crime and the cost of living.

chunks.text: A poll by Atlas released on September 29 showed the two men tied in a possible [[runoff]]. It gave Bolsonaro 47.7 percent and Lula 47.6 percent. Another poll found that [[undecided voters]] {{make up}} only 5 percent of all voters. If no candidate wins more than half of the [[valid votes]] on Sunday, the top two will {{move on to}} a runoff on October 25. The campaign has {{heated up}} this week, with both men [[trading insults]].

verbs.correct: To form a part of a total
verbs.why: Women make up half of the team. Young people make up most of the city's renters. Undecided voters make up only 5 percent of all voters, another poll found.

verbs.wrong: To share power with a rival
verbs.why: The winners move on to the next round. After the test, the class moved on to a new chapter. If no candidate wins more than half of the valid votes, the top two will move on to a runoff on October 25.
The race for mayor heated up in the final month. The debate heated up near the end. This week, the campaign has heated up, with both men trading insults.

vocab.def: To be present where you are expected
ex: Hundreds of fans showed up at the airport to meet the team.
She showed up for work an hour late.
Nobody showed up for the meeting on Friday.
The home team pulled ahead in the last few minutes.
She pulled ahead of the other swimmers on the final lap.
Our class pulled ahead in the school fundraising contest.
The two boxers will face off in Las Vegas next month.
In the debate, the candidates faced off on taxes.
Our school faces off against our biggest rival on Friday night.
Rents in the city have finally started to come down.
The price of eggs came down after the spring.
Crime in our neighborhood has come down a lot.

vocab.def: To act strongly to stop something
ex: Police are cracking down on drivers who use their phones.
The state cracked down on fake online reviews.
The airline will crack down on passengers who smoke.
The mayor set out her plan for cheaper bus fares.
The report sets out five ways to save energy.
Our boss set out the new rules in an email.
You have to stand up for yourself at work.
Her parents always stood up for her at school.
Many people stood up for the small library when the city wanted to close it.
Her honest answers won over the audience.
The company is trying to win over younger customers.
He won over my parents with his good manners.

vocab.def: To form a part of a total
ex: Students make up most of the people in this neighborhood.
Older adults make up a growing share of the country.
Salaries make up the biggest part of the school's budget.
Only four teams will move on to the playoffs.
After the warm-up, we moved on to the main exercise.
Students who pass this class can move on to the advanced level.
The fight over the new stadium is heating up.
Competition between the two phone companies heated up this year.
The argument at dinner heated up very quickly.

wordDefs.def: An election in which a whole country chooses its leaders
ex: The country will hold a general election next spring.
Turnout was high in the last general election.
The general election is held every four years.

wordDefs.def: Allowed by the rules to do or get something
ex: You are eligible for a discount if you are a student.
She will be eligible to retire next year.
Only full-time workers are eligible for the bonus.

wordDefs.def: Required by law or by a rule
ex: Wearing a helmet is compulsory on this job site.
Math is compulsory for all first-year students.
The training course is compulsory for new staff.

wordDefs.def: Money you must pay for breaking a rule or law
ex: He got a fine for parking in the wrong place.
The library charges a small fine for late books.
The company paid a large fine for polluting the river.

wordDefs.def: The fixed period of time someone holds an office
ex: The mayor is in her second term.
A US president can serve only two terms.
His term on the school board ends in June.

wordDefs.def: Not having a paid job, or the number of people without one
ex: Unemployment fell to its lowest level in ten years.
Many young people struggle with unemployment.
The factory closing caused high unemployment in the town.

wordDefs.def: A government plan that gives money or help to people in need
ex: The welfare program helps families pay for food.
She used a welfare program while she was looking for work.
The state changed the rules of its welfare program.

wordDefs.def: Help that makes a debt smaller or easier to pay
ex: Some students are hoping for debt relief on their loans.
The bank offered debt relief to customers hurt by the flood.
Debt relief gave the family a fresh start.

wordDefs.def: Risking money on games or sports using the internet
ex: He lost a lot of money on online betting.
Online betting is popular during the World Cup.
Some states have made online betting legal.

wordDefs.def: Prisons with the strictest guards and rules, for dangerous criminals
ex: Few people have ever escaped from maximum-security prisons.
The state has two maximum-security prisons in the desert.
Guards in maximum-security prisons get special training.

wordDefs.def: Taxes that a country puts on goods from other countries
ex: New tariffs made imported cars more expensive.
Farmers worry about tariffs on their exports.
The two countries agreed to lower tariffs on steel.

wordDefs.def: Money that families owe, for things like homes, cars and credit cards
ex: Household debt rose as more people used credit cards.
High household debt makes it hard for families to save.
The report shows household debt at a record level.

wordDefs.def: The amount of money needed for basic things like food and rent
ex: The cost of living in big cities keeps rising.
Her new salary barely covers the cost of living.
Many retirees move to places with a lower cost of living.

wordDefs.def: A second vote between the top two candidates when no one wins enough votes
ex: The race for mayor went to a runoff in December.
Only the top two finishers made the runoff.
Turnout was lower in the runoff than in the first vote.

wordDefs.def: Voters who have not yet chosen a candidate
ex: Both campaigns are sending ads to undecided voters.
Many undecided voters make their choice on the last day.
The debate was aimed at undecided voters.

wordDefs.def: Votes that are marked correctly and can be counted
ex: Blank ballots are not counted as valid votes.
She won 52 percent of the valid votes.
Officials checked that all valid votes were counted.

wordDefs.def: Saying rude things to each other, one after the other
ex: The two drivers were trading insults in the parking lot.
The players started trading insults during the game.
The neighbors spent the evening trading insults over the fence.

mainIdea.s: About 159 million Brazilians can vote on Sunday for a president, governors and Congress. Two of the 13 candidates lead the polls, and they are tied in a possible runoff.
mainIdea.why: The vote is on Sunday, October 4. Two of the 13 candidates have pulled ahead, and an Atlas poll showed them tied in a possible second round.

mainIdea.s: Voting is required for most adults in Brazil, and 13 people are running for president on Sunday. One new poll shows Bolsonaro far in front, so a second round looks unlikely.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the Atlas poll showed the two leading candidates tied in a possible runoff. Neither man has a big lead.

mainIdea.s: Brazil's Congress has passed a law that makes voting optional for all adults from 2028. Supporters say the change will save money, while critics fear fewer young people will vote.
mainIdea.why: Voting is still compulsory for people aged 18 to 70. The real story is Sunday's general election and the close race for president.

tf.s: Voters aged 18 to 70 who stay home have to pay a fine.
tf.why: Voting is compulsory for them, so those who do not show up on election day pay a fine.

tf.s: Thirteen candidates have pulled ahead in the polls.
tf.why: There are 13 candidates on the ballot, but only two of them have pulled ahead in the polls.

tf.s: Inflation and unemployment have come down under Lula's current government.
tf.why: Both have come down during his current term, and he has promised a more generous welfare program.

tf.s: Bolsonaro has promised to crack down on online betting.
tf.why: Lula made that promise. Bolsonaro has set out a plan to build five maximum-security prisons.

tf.s: The Atlas poll gave Lula a large lead in a possible runoff.
tf.why: It showed the two men tied, at 47.7 percent for Bolsonaro and 47.6 percent for Lula. Both are still trying to win over voters.

tf.s: Undecided voters make up only 5 percent of all voters.
tf.why: Another poll found this, so very few voters have not yet chosen a candidate.

lines.text: Did you know Brazil has a big election this Sunday?
I saw something about it. Who's running?
Thirteen people for president, but two have {{pulled ahead}}. President Lula and Bolsonaro, a senator who's the son of a former president.
So it's Lula {{facing off}} against Bolsonaro. What's Bolsonaro's main message?
Crime. He's {{set out}} a plan to build five maximum-security prisons. He wants voters to see him as [[tough on crime]].
He says inflation and unemployment have {{come down}}. He's promising more welfare and debt relief, and he wants to {{crack down on}} online betting.
What about trade with the US?
Lula says Brazil has to {{stand up for}} its independence. Bolsonaro says his good relationship with the Trump administration would protect Brazil.
One poll has them [[neck and neck]] in a runoff. It's 47.7 percent to 47.6.
Wow. So if nobody gets more than half on Sunday, the top two {{move on to}} a runoff?
Right, on October 25. And undecided voters only {{make up}} about 5 percent.
So they're both trying to {{win over}} a pretty small group. The final result is [[anybody's guess]].
Also, voting is required there for most adults. If you don't {{show up}}, you pay a fine.
Interesting. Here, voting is more of a [[civic duty]] than a rule.
And the campaign has really {{heated up}} this week. They've been trading insults.
Then I guess we'll just have to [[wait and see]] on Sunday.

expressions.def: Used about a leader who wants strong punishment for people who break the law
ex: The new governor promised to be tough on crime.
Many voters say they want a mayor who is tough on crime.

expressions.def: Used to say that two rivals are level, with neither one ahead
ex: The two teams were neck and neck until the last minute.

expressions.def: Used to say that nobody can know what will happen
ex: When the train will arrive is anybody's guess.
Who wins the game tonight is anybody's guess.

expressions.def: Something a good citizen is expected to do for the community
ex: She sees jury service as her civic duty.
My grandfather thought voting was his civic duty.

expressions.def: Used to say that we must wait to learn what happens
ex: Will it rain on the weekend? We'll have to wait and see.
